content.text: 1.2.2 Captions (Prerecorded)
Learning objectives
Identify prerecorded synchronized media, explain what captions convey, and evaluate their completeness and timing. This is a Level A criterion.
Why captions matter

A student who cannot hear a training video needs access to its spoken instructions and meaningful sounds while watching the corresponding action. Captions present the audio information as synchronized text. They include dialogue and other information necessary to understand the content, such as a warning tone or speaker identification when it is otherwise unclear. Captions are more than a full transcript shown separately: their timing connects the words and sounds to what is happening on screen.

This criterion covers prerecorded audio in synchronized media, such as a recorded demonstration with narration and moving video. WCAG's synchronized-media definition also includes audio or video synchronized with another format or time-based interactive components, subject to the defined exception for clearly labeled media alternatives for text. A podcast with a static cover and no interaction is audio-only; evaluate it under 1.2.1. A live broadcast has a separate criterion, 1.2.4.
Produce and review captions

Start with the actual soundtrack, then synchronize each caption with the corresponding speech or sound. Identify speakers where needed. Include meaningful non-speech audio, for example “[alarm sounds]” when a presenter reacts to an alarm. Avoid describing every background sound if it contributes no meaning. Check spelling, technical terms, punctuation, timing, and whether captions cover important on-screen content. Automatic speech recognition can provide a starting draft, but review and correction are necessary to establish whether the result conveys the audio accurately.

For a video saying “Select Save” while showing a button, captions that appear after the next step can make the instruction difficult to follow. In a corrected version, the text appears as the instruction is spoken. Test caption display in the intended player and make sure users can find any control needed to enable captions.
Scope and exception

The criterion excepts media that is itself a media alternative for text and is clearly labeled as such. A short summary or title does not automatically make a video an alternative for text. Review the relationship between the complete text and video. Captions do not convey visual-only information; evaluate audio description or a media alternative separately under 1.2.3 and, for Level AA, 1.2.5.
Worked example: a software demonstration

A video shows an instructor configuring an account. The instructor says, “Press Save,” a warning tone sounds, and another person says, “That setting is required.” A caption file containing only “Press Save” leaves out the warning and the second speaker's explanation. It may cause the viewer to believe the operation succeeded, even though the audio explains why it did not.

A stronger caption sequence places “Press Save” at the instruction, identifies the warning tone when it occurs, and attributes the second comment when the speaker is not apparent. Review the names of controls against the actual interface: a recognition system might render “cache” as “cash,” changing a technical instruction. If the source audio is unclear, resolve uncertainty with the producer rather than inventing speech. When the original media is edited, review the captions again; a formerly correct time code can become misaligned.
Test with the media player

Play the whole video with sound off and captions enabled. Check that meaningful audio is represented at the right time, that successive captions are readable, and that they do not hide important visual content. Then compare the captions with the soundtrack. Test the path by which a learner enables captions, including keyboard operation if a control is provided. A valid caption file that the player fails to show does not help the learner. Document identified errors and retest the corrected file.
Apply the requirement to a production change

A team adds a short introduction to an existing recorded lesson. The former captions are accurate, but they begin at the old start time. If the player displays them unchanged, each instruction now appears before the corresponding action. The content team should regenerate or adjust timings and review the entire edited recording. A quick test of the first sentence alone may miss a later edit that shifts only the final section.

Consider another video in which two people speak off camera. Captions containing their exact words can still be confusing when the discussion refers to different roles. Identify the speaker when the distinction matters, for example “[Instructor]” and “[Student].” If the source already makes the speaker clear, unnecessary repetitive labels may make the text harder to read. Similarly, “[music]” is useful when music conveys an important change of mood or covers a relevant sound; a transcript should not invent a sound or its meaning.

For implementation, inspect the player as well as the caption file. Can the learner turn captions on if they are not displayed by default? Do captions remain available when changing playback speed or seeking? These operational checks support usable delivery, while accuracy and synchronization must still be evaluated against the source. A caption track that is technically present but empty, incomplete, or out of sync cannot be treated as sufficient merely because it loads.
Required lesson activity

Use a one-minute narrated video with at least one meaningful non-speech sound. Draft synchronized captions identifying speakers when needed, then compare them with the original. Correct omissions and timing. Submit the caption text with timing notes and a brief explanation of one correction.
